1.pericope_label: After this there was a feast of the Jews

schools.summary: Gill weighs three feasts and settles on the passover; Calvin argues Pentecost from the itinerary, while declining to press it.
Henry takes the feast for the passover and gives two reasons why Christ attended, one of obedience and one of opportunity.
Ellicott argues from the chronology for Purim; Lightfoot counts this the second of the Gospel’s passovers; Barnes and Robertson hold the question undecidable.
Clarke reports the passover as the critics’ verdict and the manuscript support for the article; Wesley names Pentecost instead.
Augustine explains the attendance as a public demonstration that Christ was no enemy to the law, and as an opportunity given by the crowds.

debates.question: Which feast is meant?

sides.position: The passover
Pentecost
Purim, the only feast falling inside the chronological interval
Undeterminable, and of no consequence
The Day of Atonement

outliers.note: Alone reasons from an intercalary year with a doubled month of Adar to fix the feast as Purim, against the whole weight of the older identifications.

2.pericope_label: A pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda

schools.summary: Gill removes the word market from the text; Calvin derives the name from the conduits or from the washing of sacrificial beasts, and reads the setting as a guarantee of publicity.
Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson agree on the sheep gate and canvass the site and the manuscript forms of the name; Lightfoot explains what the Hebrew tongue meant to a first-century writer.
Wesley dates the Gospel from the present tense and guesses at the shape of the basin; Clarke doubts the argument and reports the versions that read a past tense.

debates.question: Does the present tense there is date the Gospel before the fall of Jerusalem?

sides.position: Yes, it shows the pool was still standing
No — the versions read was, and in any case the pool could outlast the city
No — it is only vivid memory

debates.question: What does the name Bethesda mean?

sides.position: House of mercy, from its healing properties
The manuscripts differ, one giving house of the olive
A name taken from the conduits, or from the washing of the sacrifices

outliers.note: Alone declines the standard etymology and reconstructs the pool as a working part of the temple water supply.

3.pericope_label: Waiting for the moving of the water; an angel went down

schools.summary: Gill rejects the sanhedrin-messenger theory and allegorises the crowd; Calvin uses the angel to argue against making angels intermediaries between God and men.

Ellicott and Robertson judge the clause and the following verse a second-century gloss and explain how it entered; Barnes keeps the angel but reduces the pool to strong medicinal water; Lightfoot confines the troubling to the feasts.
Clarke defends the disputed text and demolishes the naturalising conjecture; Wesley concedes many thought the thing natural and reads a providential purpose in it.

debates.question: Are the words about the moving of the water and the angel genuine?

sides.position: No — a gloss absent from the oldest manuscripts and rejected by modern editors
Yes — the manuscript evidence against them is not sufficient

debates.question: What produced the healing?

sides.position: A real angelic ministry, and the naturalising accounts are shifts to evade it
Medicinal water periodically agitated, the angel accounting only for the agitation
An intermittent spring, the angelic explanation being the Jews’ own and hard to credit

outliers.note: Turns a verse about angelic agency into an argument that angels must never be treated as a medium of approach to God.

schools.summary: Calvin lists the circumstances that make the miracle certain and gives the question a double purpose, toward the man and toward the witnesses; Gill fixes the place.

Ellicott measures the years and notes that this man alone was addressed first; Barnes withholds a diagnosis; Robertson presses the verb of willing and the question of how Jesus knew; Lightfoot refers the question to the sabbath.
Clarke turns the long affliction into proof against collusion and reads the question as a model for gospel preaching.
John Chrysostom uses the paralytic’s endurance to argue for the medicinal power of Scripture itself.

debates.question: Why did Christ ask a question whose answer was obvious?

sides.position: It really asks whether he would be healed on a sabbath
To excite faith, hope and desire in the sufferer
To kindle desire and to make the bystanders attend
The verb asks after the will, not the expectation

outliers.note: Reads the episode not as a healing narrative but as evidence that the Scriptures supply a remedy for every condition of soul.

7.pericope_label: Rise, take up thy bed, and walk

schools.summary: Gill notes the courtesy of the address; Calvin makes the reply a mirror of our own habit of limiting God to the means we can see, and defends the deliberate offence of the command.

Barnes and Ellicott read the reply as helplessness rather than refusal, Ellicott finding faith in it without a profession; Robertson explains the belief about the spring and marks the first sabbath collision; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic carrying rule.
Clarke reports the fuller reading of the reply, hears God speaking in the command, and lists the attesting circumstance Christ attached to his miracles; Wesley states the man’s difficulty plainly.

debates.question: Why command a man to carry his bed on the sabbath?

sides.position: Lordship over the sabbath, the man’s poverty, and a standing correction of superstitious observance
To spread the miracle and to open the way for the discourse that follows
It deliberately begins the sabbath controversy in Jerusalem

outliers.note: Answers the objection that the man showed no faith by locating faith in his persistence rather than in any words he spoke.

themes: the command and the strength to obey

10.pericope_label: It is the sabbath day: it is not lawful for thee to carry thy bed

schools.summary: Gill fixes the scene; Calvin allows that the accusation was proper in itself and locates the fault in the refusal to weigh the answer.

Ellicott reads the objection as formalism that has crushed the heart out of the law; Robertson notes the penalty and the treatment of the healing as incidental; Barnes defends the man’s inference and generalises it.
Clarke sets the healed man’s reasoning out as a formal argument from the character of his healer.

debates.question: Were the Jews wrong to raise the objection at all?

sides.position: Yes — it was cavil, and formalism blind to the miracle in front of it
No — the accusation was just and proper; the fault lay in not accepting the answer

outliers.note: Concedes the legitimacy of the challenge before condemning the challengers, and turns the episode into a rule about withholding judgement until the reason for an action is known.

12.pericope_label: He that was healed wist not who he was

schools.summary: Gill explains the man’s ignorance from the brevity of the encounter; Calvin gives the withdrawal a purpose and denies that the cure can be credited to the man’s faith.

Barnes and Ellicott read the question as evasion of the evidence; Robertson notes the contemptuous phrasing and the rare verb of withdrawal; Ellicott rejects the idea that Christ left to escape a crowd.
Clarke takes the withdrawal as prudence, since the work was unfinished and the rulers dangerous.

debates.question: Why did Jesus withdraw?

sides.position: To avoid a gathering tumult, the work being unfinished
He simply passed on with the crowd; it explains how he went unrecognised, not why he left
So that the fact might be weighed on its own before its author was known
The crowd is the stated reason for the departure

outliers.note: Turns the exchange into a general observation about controversy, that men attend only to the point of difference and never to the reasons behind it.

14.pericope_label: Sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee

schools.summary: Gill sends the man straight to the temple; Calvin reads the encounter as a lesson in gratitude rather than a diagnosis, and explains why Christ now comes forward.
Barnes and Robertson take the warning to name the cause of the illness, Robertson qualifying the principle; Ellicott presses the present imperative and weighs what could be worse.
Clarke warns against using restored health in the service of sin and finds proof of Christ’s knowledge of the past; Wesley states the causal reading briefly.
Chrysostom praises the man for going to the temple rather than to pleasure; John Chrysostom generalises that God scourges the body to heal the soul.

debates.question: Does the warning mean the man’s illness was caused by his own sin?

sides.position: Yes, and Christ names the cause he already knew
Yes in this case, though not all sickness has that cause
Yes as a general principle: the body is punished to heal the soul
The verse is about gratitude for the gift, not the aetiology of the disease

outliers.note: Alone declines to read the warning as an explanation of the illness, taking it instead as the demand that a received mercy be answered by a life of service.

15.pericope_label: Therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus

schools.summary: Calvin and Gill find the report pious and grateful rather than treacherous; Gill notes the persecution began with the tongue.

Ellicott acquits the healed man of any hostile intent and argues that the clause about seeking to slay is a later insertion; Barnes catalogues the injustice of the persecution; Robertson reads the man’s report as self-protection and marks the open breach.

Clarke observes what the man carefully did not say, defends the disputed clause, and describes religious persecution as the most dangerous of dispositions; Wesley draws the lesson for readers whose good is evil spoken of.

debates.question: What was the healed man’s motive in naming Jesus?

sides.position: Innocent, and probably hopeful that the rulers would recognise a prophet
Pious — to render his Physician the honour due
Careful: he named his healer, not the one who told him to carry the bed
Either ungrateful betrayal or incompetence, and deserving small respect either way

debates.question: Are the words and sought to slay him genuine?

sides.position: No — inserted to explain the following verse
Yes — and true of them in any case

outliers.note: Passes over the man and the text alike to ask why the publication of such a cure produced conspiracy rather than crowds.

17.pericope_label: My Father worketh hitherto, and I work

schools.summary: Gill sets the scene before the council; Calvin insists the defence is not that the sabbath law has lapsed but that works of God never broke it, circumcision being the standing parallel.
Henry marks the change of ground, from precedents in the law to the example of the Father and Christ’s own authority.

Barnes and Clarke argue from God’s unbroken providence to his exemption and the Son’s; Ellicott and Robertson show the premise was a commonplace of contemporary thought and press the possessive my; Lightfoot hears a double claim laid before the council.
Wesley states the proposition and notes that the rest of the chapter defends it.

debates.question: What exactly is the defence?

sides.position: God is exempt from the sabbath law, and so is the Son
The unbroken activity of God is a premise both sides already grant
Not that the law has lapsed, but that works of God never violated it
A claim before the council to be the Messiah, and so to be God

outliers.note: Answers the verse from the rabbinic debate over whether sonship can be predicated of the Messiah at all, rather than from the sabbath question.

schools.summary: Gill marks their resolve; Calvin explains why Christ pressed a defence that would inflame them, and distinguishes the charge they made from the truth of the case.
Ellicott and Barnes agree that the hearers read the claim rightly; Robertson traces how the sabbath grudge became a graver charge and how the hostility hardened.
Clarke lists the two capital charges now available to them; Wesley presses the untranslatable force of his own Father and notes that Christ never corrected the inference.

debates.question: Did the Jews misunderstand what Christ claimed?

sides.position: No — the inference to equality was correct, and was never withdrawn
They were right about the claim and wrong about the sabbath; the evangelist reports their opinion, not the fact

outliers.note: Converts the episode into three rules about proclaiming truth that endangers the speaker or enrages the hearer.

19.pericope_label: The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin agree that Christ concedes rather than corrects the charge; Calvin rejects both the Arian and the standard patristic reading of the verse.

Ellicott shows the words answering the charge of blasphemy and the later charge of inferiority alike; Barnes and Robertson define the dependence; Lightfoot reads it as a rabbinic maxim about the Messiah as servant.
Clarke argues that only a non-creature could be so limited, and turns it back on the sabbath charge; Wesley calls the incapacity a glory rather than a defect.
Cyril of Jerusalem grounds the saying in the Father’s will that the Son should reign over the creation he made.
Hilary makes the works of the Son the Father’s own acting in him; Augustine of Hippo describes the kind of hearing this Gospel demands.

debates.question: Do the words concede that the Son is inferior?

sides.position: Yes
No — they mark only the distinction of persons
holders: the orthodox fathers (as reported by Calvin)

sides.position: Neither answer will do; the discourse is not about the simple divinity
They prove the opposite, since only a non-creature could be incapable of acting apart from God
They answer blasphemy and inferiority together, by the relation of Son to Father
They state the obedience of the Messiah as sent servant, not any weakness

outliers.note: Opens with a note on the evangelist rather than the verse, warning that these sayings exercise larger minds and can only unsettle the unready.

20.pericope_label: The Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth

schools.summary: Gill grounds the love in the Son’s being the Father’s image; Calvin rejects the older reading that God loves himself in the Son and refers the love to Christ incarnate as Head of the church.
Barnes infers omniscience from the completeness of the showing; Ellicott pairs the Son’s inability with the Father’s necessity to impart; Robertson weighs the two Greek verbs for love.
Clarke identifies the greater works and warns that Christ speaks now as God and now as the ambassador of God; Wesley presses the simultaneity of showing and doing.
Augustine of Hippo restates the inseparability of the works of Father and Son, and sets knowing above both ignorance and error.

debates.question: Whom does the Father love, and in what capacity?

sides.position: The eternal Son, as his own image and equal
Christ clothed with flesh, chosen as Head of the church, so that the love may flow from him to us

debates.question: What are the greater works?

sides.position: Raising the dead and judging the world, named in the verses that follow
The whole unfolding of the mediatorial work, of which the healings are first signs

outliers.note: Supplies an interpretive rule for the discourse, that Christ speaks by turns as God and as God’s ambassador, and blames many errors on the failure to observe it.

21.pericope_label: The Son quickeneth whom he will

schools.summary: Gill leans to a spiritual raising on the strength of the present tense; Calvin takes the verse as declaring Christ the Author of life in the fullest sense.

Barnes and Robertson argue from the claim to equality and note it precedes any raising Christ had yet performed; Ellicott makes the works general, spiritual and physical at once, and refers the manifestation in time to the Son.
Clarke contrasts Christ’s raising at will with the prophets, who had to ask for the power; Wesley maps the structure of the discourse that follows.
Augustine denies both that the Father and Son raise different people and that the Son is an instrument, insisting that the will as well as the power is shared.

debates.question: Is the quickening bodily or spiritual?

sides.position: Chiefly spiritual, the present tense pointing to dead sinners raised now
Both at once, and present as well as future
Literal raising, of a kind the prophets performed only by request
The whole gift of life, righteousness and every part of salvation included

outliers.note: Fixes on the words whom he will to exclude any reading in which the Son is the Father’s instrument rather than a joint agent.

22.pericope_label: That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father

schools.summary: Gill supplies the missing qualification to the denial; Calvin answers the objection that the Father is thereby left idle, and makes the honour clause the rule of all worship.
Ellicott presses the emphatic denial and pairs judging with quickening; Barnes defines the honour and cites early pagan testimony to it; Robertson takes the verse as a claim to worship.
Clarke argues from equal honour to the deity of the Son and calls any lesser worship idolatry; Wesley divides the honour into willing and unwilling.
Cyril of Jerusalem guards the Father’s undiminished power and turns the judgement on the conscience; John Chrysostom urges the tribunal as a daily discipline.

debates.question: How can it be said that the Father judges no man?

sides.position: It means not without the Son; the Father has always judged through him
Emphatically: not even the Father judges, all judgement being committed to the Son
He governs in the person of the Son without ceasing to govern, since Christ is set before us because we cannot rise to God
Without divesting himself of power, he judges through the Son, whose will is one with his

outliers.note: Supports the claim to divine honour with a hostile external witness, a provincial governor’s report that Christians sang hymns to Christ as God.

24.pericope_label: He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life

schools.summary: Calvin makes obedience to the gospel the whole of the honour demanded, and calls any other profession the kiss of Judas; Gill names the swearer.
Henry treats the passage as a declaration of messianic authority covering both spiritual and bodily raising.
Ellicott and Robertson read eternal life as a present possession and correct condemnation to judgement; Barnes defines hearing as obedience rather than audition.
Clarke describes the change of state as an emigration out of the country of death; Wesley qualifies the exemption from condemnation.
Cyril of Jerusalem takes the verse for the first of two senses of faith and marvels that an hour’s belief gains what years of well-pleasing gained the ancients.
Gloss resolves the strange construction by identifying the Son with the Father’s Word; Augustine of Hippo reflects on the limits of both preacher and hearer.

debates.question: Is the exemption from judgement unconditional?

sides.position: Yes — a completed passage out of death, so that no condemnation remains
Unless the believer makes shipwreck of the faith
It holds for those who actually obey the gospel; a profession without faith is betrayal

outliers.note: Attaches a single conditional clause to a promise every other witness here reads as absolute.

25.pericope_label: The dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live

schools.summary: Calvin holds the spiritual sense and explicitly refutes the physical instances; Gill marks the continuing argument for equality.

Ellicott gives three arguments for a purely spiritual raising and Robertson concurs; Barnes refuses to choose and defends double reference from Scripture usage; Lightfoot recovers the Jewish expectation of resurrection at the Messiah’s coming.
Wesley names three literal raisings; Clarke sets out three kinds of death and three answering kinds of life without choosing between them.
Augustine reads the verse as proof that the Son quickens as the Father does, and takes now is to mean the hour is near.

debates.question: Who are the dead that hear?

sides.position: The spiritually dead only; the physical instances are refuted by what follows
Those actually raised — the ruler’s daughter, the widow’s son, Lazarus
Both, since Scripture often describes two similar events in one set of words

outliers.note: Reads the saying against rabbinic comment on the valley of dry bones, including the gloss that the bones are men without the moisture of the law.

26.pericope_label: As the Father hath life in himself, so hath he given to the Son

schools.summary: Calvin makes the possession of life the reason the voice gives life, and Christ the open fountain of a hidden source; Gill refers it to life laid up in covenant.

Barnes and Ellicott argue from underived life to the necessity of an original source in the Son; Ellicott and Robertson press the missing articles in a son of man and refer the judicial office to his humanity; Lightfoot supplies the prophetic figure behind the title.
Wesley grounds the gift in eternal generation and the judicial office in the incarnation; Clarke reads the verse of Christ as envoy and follows the older punctuation.
Cyril of Jerusalem guards the generation against any loss or lack; Theophylact refuses the common punctuation and explains why judgement is preached so insistently.

debates.question: When was life in himself given to the Son?

sides.position: By eternal generation, absolute and independent
In time, to one who had possessed it before all time, for the mediatorial work
The question is of manifestation: the hidden fountain set open in Christ

debates.question: What does because he is the Son of man govern?

sides.position: The words that follow — it cannot be the ground of judicial power
The grant of judgement, and it means his humanity rather than his messiahship
It means the Messiah of the prophet’s vision

outliers.note: Explains the insistence on judgement as a rhetorical strategy aimed at obstinate hearers rather than as doctrine for its own sake.

28.pericope_label: All that are in the graves shall hear his voice

schools.summary: Gill lists what the marvel might be and reads the coming forth by the pattern of Lazarus; Calvin defends the logic of arguing from the bodily resurrection and keeps good works from becoming a ground of merit.

Ellicott marks the absence of and now is and ties the future judgement to the present law of light and darkness; Robertson distinguishes the word for grave and finds two resurrections as to result; Barnes presses the extent and the meaning of a resurrection of life.
Wesley defines the resurrection of life in a line.

debates.question: Why appeal to the bodily resurrection at all, when raising souls is no lesser work?

sides.position: The comparison is drawn from the opinion of carnal men, who admire only what is outward
Because it is a further and greater work still to come, announced without and now is

outliers.note: Concedes that the argument concedes something to human carnality, since men wonder at raised bodies and pass over raised souls unmoved.

30.pericope_label: I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me

schools.summary: Gill treats the verse as the application of the whole argument to Christ himself; Calvin dismisses the ancient debate over what the Son hears as beside the point.
Henry reads it as a return to the declaration of agreement between Father and Son.

Ellicott grounds the justice of the judgement in its accord with the eternal will; Robertson notes the return to the first person and the simplicity of the Son’s task; Barnes defines hearing as commission; Lightfoot finds an allusion to appellate practice.
Wesley grounds the incapacity in essential union; Clarke makes the subjection of Christ’s humanity the pattern for every disciple’s will.
Augustine takes the words as anticipating an objection and weighs whether the hearing belongs to the human subordination or to the divine nature.

debates.question: What does as I hear, I judge describe?

sides.position: The condition of one commissioned and instructed
Either the human subordination or the immutable nature — both readings are open
Not the eternal divinity at all; the ancients wasted effort refuting Arius from it
The guarantee that the sentence accords with the eternal will and so is just
A judge referring a doubtful case upward and giving sentence on what he is told

outliers.note: Reads the clause through the appellate practice of the courts, where a doubting judge went up to the council and sentenced by what he heard there.

31.pericope_label: If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true

schools.summary: Calvin reads the words as a voluntary concession, a surrender of a right in order to win the argument on the opponents’ own terms; Gill supplies the rabbinic rule.
Henry takes the legal maxim as a standing reproach to human veracity.

Barnes and Robertson set the saying against the two-witness rule of ancient law, Robertson noting the paradox that elsewhere Christ affirms the opposite; Ellicott makes the verse the hinge between the person and the witnesses.
Wesley resolves it by a parenthesis, Clarke by the evidence of the miracles, and reports a proposal to read the sentence as a question.

Chrysostom states the difficulty at its sharpest and resolves it by referring true to their suspicions rather than to the testimony itself; John Chrysostom prefaces it with a warning about careless reading.

debates.question: How can Christ say his own witness is not true?

sides.position: True is said with reference to their suspicions, not to the testimony’s intrinsic worth
It is a concession: he surrenders a right he possesses
A paradox resolved by the Father as second witness
It means if he testified alone, which is impossible
The clause may be a question, not a concession at all

outliers.note: Opens with an image of unskilled mining to argue that the passage yields nothing to readers who take all Scripture in one manner.

32.pericope_label: There is another that beareth witness of me

schools.summary: Gill argues from the gradation of the discourse that the other witness is John, not the Father; Calvin turns the deputation into a charge of malice.
Ellicott, Robertson and Barnes identify the other witness as the Father and press the perfect tenses of the deputation to John; Ellicott and Barnes weigh the quality of that human testimony.
Clarke describes the Father’s witness through the prophets and lists four grounds for trusting the Baptist; Wesley appeals to the hearers’ own judgement.

debates.question: Who is another that beareth witness?

sides.position: The Father
John, the discourse rising by degrees from a man to the works and only then to the Father

debates.question: Should the verse read I know or ye know?

sides.position: I know; the origin of the variant is obvious
The variant is reported and left open, and would sharpen the reproach

outliers.note: Stands alone in reading the unnamed witness as the Baptist, on the ground that the passage ascends by stages and the Father comes last.

34.pericope_label: He was a burning and a shining light

schools.summary: Gill denies that Christ needed human testimony and describes John’s burning and shining; Calvin explains why testimony is used at all and turns the lamp into evidence of wilful blindness.
Ellicott and Barnes insist on lamp against light and explain the article; Robertson quotes the maxim that the lamp is not needed once the Light comes; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic idiom.
Clarke argues from their own estimate of John and renders the word as lamp; Wesley presses the purpose of salvation and the fact that it failed.
Cyril of Jerusalem turns the principle of the verse on his own teaching, refusing to be believed except on prophetic testimony.

debates.question: Does Christ need human testimony or not?

sides.position: He has no need of it; the works testify sufficiently
He did receive it, but it was never the foundation — only a means of leading them to himself
He uses it not because he needs it but because we profit by the confirmation

outliers.note: Applies the verse to the preacher rather than the hearer, forbidding his own congregation to accept anything from him that the prophets do not confirm.

36.pericope_label: The works which the Father hath given me to finish bear witness of me

schools.summary: Gill corrects a version that compares Christ with John rather than with his testimony; Calvin sets the verse in the argument and finds two proofs, the miracles now and the Scriptures beforehand.

Barnes identifies the works with the miracles and presses the verb of completion; Ellicott widens them to the whole messianic task; Robertson renders the comparison and notes that the highest faith needs no such proof.
Clarke grants the Baptist every honour before setting his testimony aside, and points to a thirty-eight-year cure worked by a word.

debates.question: What are the works that bear witness?

sides.position: The miracles, given him to perform until the task was complete
Not miracles only, but every part of the messianic work
Works that testify, though the highest faith does not require them

outliers.note: Qualifies the evidential argument from within, holding that Christ himself ranked a faith that needs no works above one that rests on them.

37.pericope_label: Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape

schools.summary: Calvin extends the witness over the whole history of promise; Gill weighs three senses of his word; Calvin makes the rejection of Christ proof that the word never lodged in them.

Barnes leaves the Father’s witness undecided among three and counts the charges; Ellicott rejects the heavenly voices as the reference and expounds the word that dwells in a mind; Robertson denies any audible witness and locates it in the believer’s heart.
Wesley names the baptism and disclaims Joseph; Clarke answers by the prophets and makes the negative clause a parenthesis.

debates.question: Where and when did the Father bear witness?

sides.position: Perhaps in the miracles, the baptism and the prophets together
At the baptism
Through the prophets, the denial of voice and form being a parenthesis
Not in the heavenly voices at all; the words cover the whole span of earlier revelation
In the heart of the believer, by neither audible voice nor visible form

outliers.note: Breaks off to insist that the Father he speaks of is not his reputed father, and that his hearers are strangers to the one he means.

39.pericope_label: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life

schools.summary: Gill allows both moods and describes how generally the Scriptures were read; Calvin absolves the searching and condemns the reading that finds only the dead letter.
Henry takes the words both ways and warns that study of the letter is compatible with being a stranger to its power.

Ellicott lays out the ancient dispute over mood and decides for the indicative from the parallel verbs; Lightfoot and Robertson agree; Barnes recovers the force of the verb from its use of miners, lioness and hounds.
Clarke argues the indicative from the sense of the next verse and documents the rabbinic esteem for study; Wesley calls the words a plain command to all men.
John Chrysostom presses the difference between reading and searching as the difference between careless and profitable religion.

debates.question: Is search the scriptures imperative or indicative?

sides.position: Indicative — a description of what they already do
Imperative — a plain command to all men
Either will serve, and both yield a lesson

outliers.note: Recovers the weight of the verb from its secular uses — the miner after ore, the robbed lioness after a trail, the hound after a scent.

40.pericope_label: Ye will not come to me, that ye might have life

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes bodily from spiritual coming and guards the disclaimer of honour; Calvin makes the refusal deliberate flight from the light.

Ellicott locates the hindrance in the will and warns against a merely literary study of Scripture; Barnes draws rules from the refusal and from the disclaimer of applause; Robertson names the tragedy and denies any wounded pride in Christ.
Clarke states the irony of searching for a Messiah while refusing the one pointed out, and puts the disclaimer as pure disinterest.
Chrysostom explains the disclaimer as forestalling a suspicion, and compares the sun that gains nothing from a candle.

debates.question: Why does Christ disclaim honour from men?

sides.position: Because his nature does not need it, as the sun needs no candle
To account for their unbelief rather than to defend himself
Honour is due him and given him by his own; he denies only that he sought applause here
To clear himself of pleading his own cause before pressing the charge that follows
Because ambition is no motive of his; he seeks the Father’s glory

outliers.note: Sets the refusal in the position of the men addressed, who had their own schools and disciples and were themselves called Rabbi.

42.pericope_label: I am come in my Father’s name, and ye receive me not

schools.summary: Gill grounds the knowledge in omniscience and defines coming in the Father’s name as a commissioned mission; Calvin makes the phrase a standing test of true and false teachers.

Robertson presses the perfect tense and the objective genitive; Ellicott turns their own confession of the first commandment against them and traces the rejection to want of love; Barnes describes the rival kind of teacher.
Clarke denies that zeal for God’s honour is the real motive and explains the rabbinic convention of teaching in another’s name; Wesley hears compassion in the rebuke.
Cyril of Jerusalem reads the clause as a prophecy already being fulfilled in an expectation of the deceiver.

debates.question: What is meant by coming in his own name?

sides.position: A teacher setting up himself with no pretence of divine commission
A breach of the rabbinic rule that a teacher cite an authority before him
The mark that separates lawful teachers of the church from the spurious
The deceiver still awaited by those who refused the Messiah

outliers.note: Argues that continuity, not conversion, was the issue: the true Israelite became the true Christian, and these men had never been true members of the old covenant.

44.pericope_label: How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another?

schools.summary: Gill itemises the habits of honour-seeking; Calvin answers the charge of harshness by naming ambition as the thing that shuts the gate of faith.
Ellicott and Robertson make the impossibility a matter of what the hearers already are; Barnes traces the refusal to an expectation of a splendid Messiah and generalises it to all unbelief.
Clarke prices the choice exactly, reputation against the soul; Wesley notes the festival at which the words would have stung most.

debates.question: In what sense could they not believe?

sides.position: Not at all, while they remain what they are; the two positions are incompatible
They were unwilling, expecting a Messiah of pomp and refusing a humble one
They made a deliberate exchange, choosing reputation over the soul
Ambition had already deprived them of sound judgement

outliers.note: Places the saying at the feast commemorating the giving of the law, when sermons in praise of that law and its people were at their height.

themes: the glory that is from God

45.pericope_label: There is one that accuseth you, even Moses, in whom ye trust

schools.summary: Gill denies the office of accuser to Christ altogether; Calvin makes the summoning of the hardened to God’s judgement-seat a rule of pastoral practice, and grounds the accusation in contempt of a prophet’s doctrine.
Henry generalises the failure to every trust in a form of doctrine that is never entered into.

Barnes and Robertson read the disclaimer as a refusal to imitate the accusers and press the legal force of the verb; Ellicott denies that love can accuse and turns the accusation inward; Ellicott and Robertson differ on whether the witness of Moses lies in particular texts or in the whole.

Clarke sets out the counter-charge Christ declines to make, reports the maxim that only Moses could accuse them, and lists both the express prophecies and the sacrificial system; Wesley answers in four words, by his writings.

debates.question: In what sense does Moses accuse them?

sides.position: By his writings, which foretold the Messiah and commanded them to hear him
Because they despise his doctrine, and every prophet has a commission to confound the unbelieving
No one accuses them; the heart that refuses light accuses and condemns itself

debates.question: Where did Moses write of Christ?

sides.position: In express prophecies, and in the symbols and the whole sacrificial system
Chiefly in the promise of a prophet like himself
Not in particular passages, but in the whole spirit of the books

outliers.note: Refuses the whole notion of an accuser, arguing that light condemns simply by shining and the heart passes sentence on itself.

47.pericope_label: If ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes believing the books from believing what they contain; Calvin explains why Christ seems to rank Moses above himself and finds the comparison an aggravation of their guilt.

Barnes draws four rules from the argument from greater to less; Robertson weighs the two terms and the range of the word for writings; Ellicott shifts the emphasis from the terms to the possessives and reads the verse as the previous one advanced in time.
Clarke presses the prejudice that blocks the lesser testimony once the greater is refused.

debates.question: Does the sentence rank Moses above Christ?

sides.position: It accommodates itself to hearers for whom the law was the supreme authority; Christ could not in fact be the inferior
The contrast is not between writings and words but between his and mine
The authority of Moses was simply the greatest that people acknowledged

outliers.note: Ends on the rule that rejection is indivisible: whoever refuses one part of Scripture will refuse the rest on the same grounds.
